claims.source: While sirenians do not possess the capacity for non-shivering thermogenesis due to pseudogenization of the UCP1 gene (Gaudry et al., 2017), the reduced Hb-O2 affinity shift in Steller's sea cow Hb was speculated to have promoted increased O2 offloading to fuel increased thermogenesis to help cope with exposure to cold sub-Arctic waters.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous genetic study.

claims.claim: Steller's sea cow Hb accumulated 11 amino acid replacements since its divergence from the dugong.
claims.source: Although the Hb of this species accumulated 11 amino acid replacements since its divergence from the dugong (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), this decrease in Hb-O2 affinity was hypothesized to arise from a highly unusual 82Lys→Asn exchange in the chimeric beta-type (β/δ) chain (Signore et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and cited from previous work.

claims.claim: The β/δ82Lys→Asn substitution was fixed in the last remaining Steller's sea cow population.
claims.source: Data mined from more recent ancient DNA studies (Le Duc et al., 2022; Sharko et al., 2021) confirms that this substitution was fixed in the last remaining Steller's sea cow population (Figure 1B), though the specific functional effect(s) of this substitution have not been characterized.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through sequence data from 16 individuals shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Human Hb Providence (β82Lys→Asn) variant exhibits decreased inherent Hb-O2 affinity and markedly reduced sensitivity to DPG, Cl−, and H+.
claims.source: For example, the human Hb Providence (β82Lys→Asn) variant exhibits a decreased inherent Hb-O2 affinity and markedly reduced sensitivity to the allosteric effectors 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (DPG), Cl−, and H+ (Abraham et al., 2011; Bardakjian et al., 1985; Bonaventura et al., 1976; Charache et al., 1977; Weickert et al., 1999), all of which preferentially bind and stabilize the (low O2 affinity) deoxy-state conformation of the protein.
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on human Hb Providence.

claims.claim: The β/δ82Lys→Asn replacement deletes integral binding sites for Cl− and DPG.
claims.source: Hence, the H. gigas β/δ82Lys→Asn replacement, which deletes integral binding sites for the heterotropic ligands Cl− and DPG (Bonaventura et al., 1976), is puzzling in that it is expected to maladaptively increase the effect of temperature on O2 uptake and release in the blood of the sub-Arctic Steller's sea cow.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation and structural modeling shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The P50 of Steller's sea cow Hb (8.8 mm Hg) is approximately 2 times higher than that of dugong (3.5 mm Hg), ancestral dugongid (4.3 mm Hg), and manatee (5.4 mm Hg) Hbs in the absence of allosteric effectors at pH 7.2 and 37°C.
claims.source: In the absence of allosteric effectors (pH 7.2, 37°C), the P50 (the O2 tension resulting in 50% Hb-O2 saturation) of Steller's sea cow Hb (P50=8.8 mm Hg) is ~2 times higher than that of dugong (3.5 mm Hg), ancestral dugongid (4.3 mm Hg), and manatee (5.4 mm Hg) Hbs under the same conditions (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary file 1a).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental O2 equilibrium measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The increased intrinsic P50 of Steller's sea cow Hb predominantly arises from the β/δ82Asn substitution.
claims.source: Site-directed mutagenesis experiments reveal that the increased intrinsic P50 of Steller's sea cow Hb predominantly arises from the β/δ82Asn substitution, as the β/δ82Asn→Lys mutant exhibits an intrinsic P50 similar to that of the ancestral dugongid (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through site-directed mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The O2 affinity of dugong, ancestral dugongid, and manatee Hbs was reduced in the presence of Cl− and DPG by a similar degree to that of Asian elephant Hb.
claims.source: Of note, the O2 affinity of dugong, ancestral dugongid, and manatee Hbs was reduced in the presence of Cl− and DPG (P50=10.2, 9.9, and 10.9 mm Hg, respectively) by a similar degree to that of Asian elephant Hb (Campbell et al., 2010a).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental measurements and comparison with cited literature.

claims.claim: The high O2 affinity of dugong and manatee blood is not attributable to decreased allosteric effector sensitivity.
claims.source: This finding extends previous studies conducted on sirenian Hbs (Farmer et al., 1979; McCabe et al., 1978; Signore et al., 2019), and reveals that the high O2 affinity of dugong and manatee blood is not attributable to decreased allosteric effector sensitivity.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental measurements showing normal allosteric responses.

claims.claim: Steller's sea cow Hb exhibits lower DPG, Cl−, and H+ (Bohr) effects relative to those of the ancestral dugongid and β/δ82Asn→Lys mutant.
claims.source: When the effects of these allosteric effectors were measured individually, Steller's sea cow Hb exhibits lower DPG, Cl−, and H+ (Bohr) effects relative to those of the ancestral dugongid and β/δ82Asn→Lys mutant (Figure 2C–E, Supplementary file 1a).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental measurements shown in Figure 2C-E.

claims.claim: A high intrinsic Hb-O2 affinity is an ancient sirenian trait that likely aided the transition of the group to the aquatic environment.
claims.source: These data confirm that a high intrinsic (i.e. in the absence of allosteric effectors) Hb-O2 affinity is an ancient sirenian trait that likely aided the transition of the group to the aquatic environment, and that Hb-O2 (and hence whole blood) affinity was secondarily reduced in the Steller's sea cow lineage (Signore et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from comparative measurements showing high affinity in ancestral dugongid and extant sirenians.

claims.claim: Hb-O2 affinity was secondarily reduced in the Steller's sea cow lineage.
claims.source: These data confirm that a high intrinsic (i.e. in the absence of allosteric effectors) Hb-O2 affinity is an ancient sirenian trait that likely aided the transition of the group to the aquatic environment, and that Hb-O2 (and hence whole blood) affinity was secondarily reduced in the Steller's sea cow lineage (Signore et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through comparative measurements showing higher P50 in H. gigas compared to ancestral dugongid.

claims.claim: The secondary reduction in blood O2 affinity in Steller's sea cow contrasts with allometric expectations for mammals.
claims.source: This latter finding contrasts with allometric expectations for mammals—whereby blood O2 affinity and body mass are inversely correlated (Schmidt-Neilsen and Larimer, 1958)—and thus further suggests this modification served an adaptive function in this extinct species.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from comparison with allometric expectations cited from literature.

claims.claim: Steller's sea cow Hb exhibits a ΔH' value (–18.8 kJ mol–1 O2) that is close to that of mammoth Hb (–17.2 kJ mol–1 O2).
claims.source: Conversely, Steller's sea cow Hb lacks heterotropic binding of DPG and displays lower Bohr (H+) and Cl− effects than all other sirenian Hbs measured (Figure 2 and Supplementary file 1a), yet exhibits a ΔH' value (–18.8 kJ mol–1 O2; Figure 2B) that is close to that of mammoth Hb (–17.2 kJ mol–1 O2) (Campbell et al., 2010a).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental measurements shown in Figure 2B and comparison with cited literature.

claims.claim: The low thermal sensitivity of H. gigas Hb largely arises from the inherently low ΔH of stripped Steller's sea cow Hb (–34.2 kJ mol–1 O2) relative to dugong, ancestral dugongid, and manatee Hbs (range: –50.1 to –58.6 kJ mol–1 O2) at pH 7.8.
claims.source: This striking convergence largely arises from the inherently low ΔH of stripped Steller's sea cow Hb (–34.2 kJ mol–1 O2) relative to dugong, ancestral dugongid, and manatee Hbs (range: –50.1 to –58.6 kJ mol–1 O2) at pH 7.8—where oxygenation-linked binding of protons is minimal—and indicates that structural differences modifying the T→R transition largely underlie the low thermal sensitivity of H. gigas Hb.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental measurements at different pH values.

claims.claim: Substitutions at position β82 are a key factor underlying the inherently low ΔH of Steller's sea cow Hb.
claims.source: Our experiments with the Steller's sea cow β82Asn→Lys mutant further implicate substitutions at this position as a key factor underlying the inherently low ΔH of the protein, as this modified protein displays a greatly increased ΔH in the absence of allosteric effectors relative to the wild-type Hydrodamalis protein (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through site-directed mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The β82Asn substitution uncouples thermal sensitivity from DPG concentration, permanently conferring the H. gigas protein with a numerically low ΔH'.
claims.source: These data suggest that β82Asn uncouples thermal sensitivity from DPG concentration, permanently conferring the H. gigas protein with a numerically low ΔH' by genetic assimilation while simultaneously eliminating the energetic cost of DPG production within the red blood cells.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from experimental data showing similar ΔH' values for wild-type and mutant H. gigas Hb in the presence of allosteric effectors despite different intrinsic ΔH values.

claims.claim: Previous work failed to provide evidence for positive selection or an accelerated amino acid substitution rate for any globin loci in the Steller's sea cow branch.
claims.source: Given both the marked functional changes observed for H. gigas Hb and the correspondingly large ecological and thermal shifts encountered by ancestral hydrodamaline sea cows following their exploitation of the North Pacific in the Miocene (Heritage and Seiffert, 2022), it is surprising that previous work failed to provide evidence for positive selection or an accelerated amino acid substitution rate for any globin loci in the Steller's sea cow branch (Signore et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is based on citation to previous phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: The Hb coding genes of woolly mammoths and stem penguins lack statistically significant signatures of positive selection despite clear directional changes in their Hb properties.
claims.source: However, this result is not unique to hydrodamalines, as the Hb coding genes of woolly mammoths and stem penguins also lack statistically significant signatures of positive selection accompanying their niche transitions despite clear directional changes in their Hb properties (Campbell et al., 2010a; Signore et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on other species.

claims.claim: Steller's sea cows had a protective thick bark-like hide and extensive blubber layer.
claims.source: For example, their protective thick bark-like hide and extensive blubber layer give credence to the extreme nature of their shallow rocky and (during winter) ice-strewn habitat (Le Duc et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is based on historical accounts by Steller and cited genetic studies.

claims.claim: Steller's sea cows used fingerless, bristle-covered forelimbs for support and to shear algae and seagrasses from the rocks.
claims.source: Here, as Steller (Steller, 1751) remarked, they used fingerless, bristle-covered forelimbs for support and to shear 'algae and seagrasses from the rocks,' which they masticated 'not with teeth, which they lack altogether, but with' large, ridged keratinized pads located on the upper palate and lower mandible.
claims.evidence: This is based on historical observations by Steller cited in the text.

claims.claim: Steller's sea cows lacked teeth and instead masticated food with large, ridged keratinized pads located on the upper palate and lower mandible.
claims.source: Here, as Steller (Steller, 1751) remarked, they used fingerless, bristle-covered forelimbs for support and to shear 'algae and seagrasses from the rocks,' which they masticated 'not with teeth, which they lack altogether, but with' large, ridged keratinized pads located on the upper palate and lower mandible.
claims.evidence: This is based on historical observations by Steller cited in the text.

claims.claim: Steller's sea cows became visibly thin during winter when their spinous processes could be seen.
claims.source: Although they became visibly thin during winter when 'their spinous processes can be seen,' Steller (Steller, 1751) noted that '(t)hese animals are very voracious, and eat incessantly' such that their stupendous stomach ('6 feet [1.8 m] long, 5 feet [1.5 m] wide') and enormous intestines—which measured a remarkable 5958 inches (~151.5 m) from the esophagus to anus, equivalent to '20½ times as long as the whole animal'—is constantly 'stuffed with food and seaweed.'
claims.evidence: This is based on historical observations by Steller cited in the text.

claims.claim: Steller's sea cow intestines measured approximately 151.5 m from the esophagus to anus, equivalent to 20½ times as long as the whole animal.
claims.source: Although they became visibly thin during winter when 'their spinous processes can be seen,' Steller (Steller, 1751) noted that '(t)hese animals are very voracious, and eat incessantly' such that their stupendous stomach ('6 feet [1.8 m] long, 5 feet [1.5 m] wide') and enormous intestines—which measured a remarkable 5958 inches (~151.5 m) from the esophagus to anus, equivalent to '20½ times as long as the whole animal'—is constantly 'stuffed with food and seaweed.'
claims.evidence: This is based on historical observations by Steller cited in the text.

claims.claim: The proportionally larger gut of Steller's sea cow is consistent with higher energetic requirements relative to extant manatees.
claims.source: The proportionally larger gut (Domning, 2022) is consistent with Steller's sea cow's higher energetic requirements relative to extant manatees, which, owing to their low metabolic intensities become cold-stressed and die if chronically exposed to water temperatures below 15 °C (O'Shea et al., 1985).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from anatomical observations and comparison with extant manatees cited from literature.

claims.claim: Extant manatees become cold-stressed and die if chronically exposed to water temperatures below 15 °C.
claims.source: The proportionally larger gut (Domning, 2022) is consistent with Steller's sea cow's higher energetic requirements relative to extant manatees, which, owing to their low metabolic intensities become cold-stressed and die if chronically exposed to water temperatures below 15 °C (O'Shea et al., 1985).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous study.

claims.claim: Reductions in blood-O2 affinity accompanying the H. gigas β/δ82Lys→Asn substitution would have augmented tissue O2 delivery without tangible effects on lung O2 uptake.
claims.source: Reductions in blood-O2 affinity accompanying the H. gigas β/δ82Lys→Asn substitution are expected to have further augmented tissue O2 delivery without tangible effects on lung O2 uptake, thereby helping to fuel thermogenesis and maintain a stable core temperature.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the functional properties of the Hb measured experimentally.

claims.claim: Steller observed submergence times of 4–5 minutes for Steller's sea cows.
claims.source: Although the attendant increase in the rate of O2 consumption would have mandated a reduction in breath-hold endurance—likely reflecting the relatively short submergence times (4–5 min) observed by Steller, 1751—our results suggest that this may have been partially counteracted by an elevated blood-O2 carrying capacity that was potentially coupled to a greater lung volume (Domning, 2022).
claims.evidence: This is based on historical observations by Steller cited in the text.

claims.claim: Steller's sea cows could reach up to 11,000 kg in mass and 10 m in length.
claims.source: A final compelling aspect of Steller's sea cow evolution was their immense size—up to 11,000 kg in mass and 10 m in length—relative to extant sirenians (Domning, 1976).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous study.

claims.claim: Steller's sea cow calves weighed 1200 pounds (544 kg) and upwards.
claims.source: While Steller does not provide measurements of 'their tender little offspring,' Gerhard Friedrich Müller, who edited Steller's manuscript prior to publication, noted calves 'weighed 1200 pounds [544 kg] and upwards' (Mueller, 1761).
claims.evidence: This is based on historical account cited in the text.

claims.claim: Steller's sea cow calf mass is approximately 10–50 times the mass of newborn manatees and dugongs (~10–50 kg).
claims.source: This value is ~10–50 times the mass of newborn manatees and dugongs (~10–50 kg) (Odell, 2009) and is suggestive of rapid prenatal growth during the ~1 year gestational period indicated by Steller (Steller, 1751).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with cited data on extant sirenians.

claims.claim: At two weeks post-conception, developing human embryos begin expressing genes at the 5' end of the α (HBZ) and β (HBE) clusters to form Hb Gower I, ζ2ε2.
claims.source: Thus, at two weeks post-conception, developing human embryos begin expressing genes at the 5' end of the α (HBZ) and β (HBE) clusters, which are translated into ζ- and ε-globin chains, respectively, to form Hb Gower I, ζ2ε2 (Fantoni et al., 1981).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous study on human development.

claims.claim: At week four of human development, expression of the downstream HBA and HBG loci add α- and γ-chains to generate additional Hb isoforms including HbF (α2γ2).
claims.source: At week four, expression of the downstream HBA and HBG loci add α- and γ-chains to the erythrocytes of the developing circulatory system to generate additional Hb isoforms including HbF (α2γ2) (Hecht et al., 1966).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous study on human development.

claims.claim: The temporal production of Hb isoforms during development results in successively lower O2 affinities, which facilitates O2 transfer from maternal to embryonic and fetal blood.
claims.source: Notably, this pattern of gene expression switching during development results in the temporal production of Hb isoforms with successively lower O2 affinities (i.e. each Hb isoform has a lower O2 affinity than the protein it replaced), which facilitates O2 transfer from maternal to embryonic and fetal blood (Carter, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous review.

claims.claim: In most mammals (except bovid artiodactyls and simian primates), the expression of embryonic Hb isoforms is limited to the embryonic stage of development.
claims.source: In all mammalian lineages examined to date, with the exception of bovid artiodactyls (e.g. goats, sheep, and cows) and simian primates, the expression of the above Hb isoforms is thought to be limited to the embryonic stage of development (Carter, 2015); as such, most mammals express the same Hb isoform (HbA) during both the fetal and post-natal stages of development.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous review.

claims.claim: Blood from a 5 month-old elephant fetus contains two distinct Hb components, although only a single (adult) Hb component is present in 12-month-old fetal and adult blood.
claims.source: For example, blood from a 5 month-old elephant fetus was shown to contain two distinct Hb components, although only a single (adult) Hb component is present in 12-month-old fetal and adult blood (Riegel et al., 1967).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous study on elephants.

claims.claim: The blood of manatee calves contains a second isoHb comprising approximately 5% of total Hb.
claims.source: Likewise, the blood of manatee calves contains a second isoHb (comprising ~5% of total Hb; Farmer et al., 1979), which moreover appears to exhibit O2 binding properties distinct from that of maternal blood (White et al., 1976).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on manatees.

claims.claim: The P50 of H. gigas Gower I in the combined presence of Cl- and DPG is markedly less than adult Steller's sea cow Hb (3.1 vs. 15.2 mm Hg, respectively).
claims.source: As expected, the P50 of H. gigas Gower I in the combined presence of Cl- and DPG is markedly less than adult Steller's sea cow Hb (3.1 vs. 15.2 mm Hg, respectively) (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental O2 equilibrium measurements shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The Hb-O2 affinity of Steller's sea cow and dugong HbF (P50 of 0.56 and 1.2 mm Hg, respectively) are substantially higher than that of their respective adult counterparts.
claims.source: Similarly, the Hb-O2 affinity of Steller's sea cow and dugong HbF (P50 of 0.56 and 1.2 mm Hg, respectively) are substantially higher than that of their respective adult counterparts and, unexpectedly, also higher than that of Steller's sea cow Gower I (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental O2 equilibrium measurements shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The Bohr and cooperativity coefficients of the sirenian Gower I and HbF proteins are substantially lower than that of the post-natal (HbA) isoform.
claims.source: In line with the embryonic expressed Hb isoforms of other mammals (Brittain, 2002; Weber et al., 1987), the Bohr and cooperativity coefficients of the sirenian Gower I and HbF proteins were also substantially lower than that of the post-natal (HbA) isoform (Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1b).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental measurements and comparison with cited literature.

claims.claim: The upstream HBG transcriptional control motif ('CACCC') crucial for the suppression of human HBB gene expression during the fetal stage is mutated in both dugongs and Steller's sea cows.
claims.source: Although it remains possible that expression of these isoforms lingers into late fetal development, the upstream HBG transcriptional control motif ('CACCC') crucial for the suppression of human HBB gene expression during the fetal stage (Perez-Stable and Costantini, 1990) is mutated in both dugongs and Steller's sea cows (but not manatees or elephants; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through sequence analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The primary (if not sole) Hb isoform expressed within both the fetal and post-natal circulation of dugongids is almost certainly HbA.
claims.source: Consequently, the primary (if not sole) Hb isoform expressed within both the fetal and post-natal circulation of dugongids is almost certainly HbA.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the mutation in the CACCC motif that would prevent fetal suppression of HBB.

claims.claim: Steller's sea cow HbF exhibits a distinctly higher O2 affinity but lower cooperativity than dugong HbF.
claims.source: Intriguingly, however, Steller's sea cow HbF exhibits a distinctly higher O2 affinity but lower cooperativity than dugong HbF, traits that are likely attributed to two exceedingly rare γ-chain amino acid replacements positioned within the interior of the protein (γ38Thr→Ile and γ101Glu→Asp; Figure 4B–E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental measurements and structural modeling shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The central cavity γ101Glu→Asp replacement alters the sliding interface between the α1γ2 dimer subunits by forming a hydrogen bond with γ104Arg.
claims.source: Briefly, the central cavity γ101Glu→Asp replacement alters the highly conserved sliding interface between the α1γ2 dimer subunits by forming a hydrogen bond with γ104Arg (Figure 4B) and has been shown to increase the intrinsic affinity of human Hb Potomac (β101Glu→Asp) (Charache et al., 1978; Shih et al., 1985).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through structural modeling shown in Figure 4B and supported by citations to studies on human Hb variants.

claims.claim: Residue γ38 is located along the α2γ1 sliding interface and is in contact with the distal heme.
claims.source: Residue γ38 is also potentially functionally relevant as it is located along the α2γ1 sliding interface and is in contact the distal heme (Figure 4D; Ropero et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through structural modeling shown in Figure 4D and supported by citation.

claims.claim: The mRNA capping site of H. gigas HbF exhibits an A→G transversion mutation that has been shown to lower transcript levels of human HBB by twofold.
claims.source: Of note, however, the mRNA capping site of H. gigas HbF exhibits an A→G transversion mutation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) that has been shown to lower transcript levels of human HBB by twofold (Myers et al., 1986).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through sequence analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and supported by citation to human study.

claims.claim: DPG generally occurs in equimolar concentrations to Hb.
claims.source: This intracellular effector generally occurs in equimolar concentrations to Hb (Bunn, 1980) and strongly decreases the O2 affinity of most mammalian Hbs via direct electrostatic interactions with β2His and β82Lys (Figure 3A), together with potential water-mediated interactions with β143His and the α-NH2 group of 1Val of the β2 chain (Richard et al., 1993).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: β82Lys is strongly cationic and able to bind DPG across the entire physiological pH range.
claims.source: However, unlike the other (ionizable) residues whose ability to interact with DPG is highly pH dependent, β82Lys is strongly cationic and thus is able to bind DPG across the entire physiological pH range.
claims.evidence: This is based on established biochemical knowledge of lysine properties.

claims.claim: β82Lys is uniformly conserved in mammalian Hbs with the exception of several heterozygous adult human HbA carriers with substitutions at this position.
claims.source: Presumably arising from this indispensable role in DPG binding, this residue is uniformly conserved in mammalian Hbs (Figure 3A), with the exception of several heterozygous adult human HbA carriers with substitutions at this position (Ikkala et al., 1976; Moo-Penn et al., 1976; Sugihara et al., 1985).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through sequence conservation analysis shown in Figure 3A and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Reversion of β/δ82Asn→Lys in the Steller's sea cow mutant restores the DPG effect to the same level observed in ancestral dugongid Hb.
claims.source: This conclusion is further supported by our measurements on the Steller's sea cow β/δ82Asn→Lys mutant, which shows that reversion to the ancestral state restores the DPG effect to the same level observed in ancestral dugongid Hb (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through site-directed mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: H. gigas Hb exhibits a distinctly lower DPG effect than human Hb Providence despite possessing identical DPG binding site residues.
claims.source: Notably, and despite possessing the identical DPG binding site residues as Hb Providence, the H. gigas protein exhibits a distinctly lower DPG effect than this human variant (ΔlogP50(DPG-stripped)=0.08; Bonaventura et al., 1976; Bardakjian et al., 1985).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through comparison of experimental measurements with cited literature values.

claims.claim: The lower DPG sensitivity of Steller's sea cow Hb implicates an epistatic contribution from other amino acids in the vicinity of the DPG pocket.
claims.source: The lower DPG sensitivity of Steller's sea cow Hb thus implicates an epistatic contribution from other amino acids in the vicinity of the DPG pocket.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the difference in DPG effect between H. gigas and human Hb Providence despite identical residues at position 82.

claims.claim: The Lys→Asn replacement in the DPG binding pocket causes the O2 affinity of human HbA to increase in the presence of allosteric cofactors.
claims.source: Importantly, the Lys→Asn replacement in the DPG binding pocket causes the O2 affinity of human HbA to increase in the presence of allosteric cofactors (Bardakjian et al., 1985; Charache et al., 1977), whereas results presented in Figure 2A show Steller's sea cow Hb-O2 affinity is reduced relative to its ancestors carrying β/δ82Lys under all test conditions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on human Hb Providence and comparison with experimental data in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Both the direction and overall phenotypic effect of specific amino acid substitutions may be conditional on the genetic background in which they occur.
claims.source: This observation highlights a growing body of research indicating that both the direction and overall phenotypic effect of specific amino acid substitutions may be conditional on the genetic background in which they occur (Natarajan et al., 2023; Storz, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to recent research on epistasis.

claims.claim: Red blood cell DPG concentrations of species with suppressed DPG sensitivities are markedly reduced relative to mammals whose Hb-O2 affinity is regulated by DPG (<0.1–1.0 mM vs. 4–10 mM, respectively).
claims.source: Nonetheless, red blood cell DPG concentrations of species with suppressed DPG sensitivities are markedly reduced relative to mammals whose Hb-O2 affinity is regulated by DPG (<0.1–1.0 mM vs. 4–10 mM, respectively; Bunn, 1980).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous review.

claims.claim: Approximately 20% of glucose uptake by human erythrocytes is diverted to DPG synthesis via the Rapport-Luebering shunt.
claims.source: While the potential benefits of a low DPG sensitivity phenotype have been debated (Campbell et al., 2010b; Kay, 1977), approximately 20% of glucose uptake by human erythrocytes is diverted to DPG synthesis via the Rapport-Luebering shunt (Duhm et al., 1968), thereby bypassing production of both ATP molecules generated via the anaerobic substrate level phosphorylation pathway (Bunn, 1980; Kauffman et al., 2002; Rapoport and Luebering, 1950).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on human erythrocyte metabolism.

claims.claim: Each molecule of DPG produced comes at the expense of producing an ATP molecule.
claims.source: Accordingly, since each molecule of DPG produced comes at the expense of producing an ATP molecule, the probability that Steller's sea cow blood similarly contained low levels of this organophosphate is high.
claims.evidence: This is based on established biochemical knowledge of the Rapport-Luebering shunt.

claims.claim: Ectopic expression of human Hb Providence β82Asp mutants in E. coli increases soluble protein production by 47–116% relative to the expression of human Hb variants not carrying this substitution.
claims.source: Ectopic expression of human Hb Providence β82Asp mutants in E. coli has been shown to increase soluble protein production by 47–116% relative to the expression of human Hb variants not carrying this substitution (Weickert et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous study.

claims.claim: Steller's sea cow Hb is more soluble than those of other sirenians and the engineered H. gigas β/δ82Asn→Lys mutant.
claims.source: Consistent with this observation, we found that Steller's sea cow Hb is more soluble than those of other sirenians and the engineered H. gigas β/δ82Asn→Lys mutant (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through ammonium sulfate precipitation assays shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: Hb Providence variants exhibit sharp reductions in irreversible oxidative damage of nearby β93Cys that initiates Hb denaturation.
claims.source: While the precise mechanism underlying this phenomenon is unknown, Hb Providence variants exhibit sharp reductions in irreversible oxidative damage of nearby β93Cys that initiates Hb denaturation (Abraham et al., 2011; Jana et al., 2020; Strader et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on Hb Providence.

claims.claim: β82 replacements decrease the rate of Hb turnover and increase the half-life of the protein.
claims.source: These β82 replacements thereby presumably decrease the rate of Hb turnover and increase the half-life of the protein (Strader et al., 2017), which may contribute to the mild polycythemia in humans carrying this substitution (Bardakjian et al., 1985; Moo-Penn et al., 1976).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Humans carrying the β82 substitution exhibit mild polycythemia.
claims.source: These β82 replacements thereby presumably decrease the rate of Hb turnover and increase the half-life of the protein (Strader et al., 2017), which may contribute to the mild polycythemia in humans carrying this substitution (Bardakjian et al., 1985; Moo-Penn et al., 1976).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claims.claim: Blood with an elevated O2 carrying capacity is typical of most mammalian divers.
claims.source: Blood with an elevated O2 carrying capacity is typical of most mammalian divers, where it increases onboard O2 stores and extends dive times (Ponganis, 2011), but is not observed in extant sirenians (Farmer et al., 1979; White et al., 1976; Wong et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Elevated O2 carrying capacity is not observed in extant sirenians.
claims.source: Blood with an elevated O2 carrying capacity is typical of most mammalian divers, where it increases onboard O2 stores and extends dive times (Ponganis, 2011), but is not observed in extant sirenians (Farmer et al., 1979; White et al., 1976; Wong et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on sirenians.

claims.claim: The inherent energy change associated with forming the weak covalent bond between O2 and the heme iron (ΔHO2) is exothermic (–59 kJ mol–1 O2).
claims.source: The invariant energy change associated with forming the weak covalent bond between O2 and the heme iron (i.e. the enthalpy of heme oxygenation; ΔHO2) is exothermic (–59 kJ mol–1 O2) (Atha and Ackers, 1974), and only moderately opposed by the endothermic solubilization of O2 (ΔHH2O; 12.55 kJ mol–1 O2), resulting in an inverse relationship between temperature and Hb-O2 affinity.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous thermodynamic study.

claims.claim: Hbs with numerically low ΔH' values are interpreted to be adaptive for cold-tolerant, regionally heterothermic mammals.
claims.source: By facilitating adequate oxygenation of cool peripheral tissues, Hbs with numerically low ΔH' values is interpreted to be adaptive for cold-tolerant, regionally heterothermic mammals.
claims.evidence: This is based on established understanding of Hb thermal adaptation.

claims.claim: The evolution of low ΔH' phenotype has predominantly been attributed to the formation of additional heterotropic ligand binding sites on the protein moiety.
claims.source: The evolution of this phenotype has predominantly been attributed to the formation of additional heterotropic ligand binding sites on the protein moiety, as has previously been demonstrated for the woolly mammoth, Mammuthus primigenius (Campbell et al., 2010a; Weber and Campbell, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on woolly mammoth.

claims.claim: A large positive ΔHT→R may contribute to the low ΔH' of deer mouse, cow, shrew, and mole Hbs.
claims.source: Recent studies have shown that a large positive ΔHT→R may similarly contribute to the low ΔH' of deer mouse, cow, shrew, and mole Hbs (Campbell et al., 2010b; Campbell et al., 2012; Jensen et al., 2016; Signore et al., 2012; Weber et al., 2014) suggesting that this potential mechanism of temperature adaptation may be more widespread than previously appreciated.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on various mammalian species.

claims.claim: The β82Asn substitution uncouples thermal sensitivity from DPG concentration by genetic assimilation.
claims.source: These data suggest that β82Asn uncouples thermal sensitivity from DPG concentration, permanently conferring the H. gigas protein with a numerically low ΔH' by genetic assimilation while simultaneously eliminating the energetic cost of DPG production within the red blood cells.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from experimental data showing similar ΔH' values despite different DPG responses.

claims.claim: The β82Asn residue of human Hb Providence slowly undergoes post-translational deamidation in vivo to form aspartic acid, with the latter residue comprising approximately 67–75% in mature mixed blood.
claims.source: It should be noted that the β82Asn residue of human Hb Providence is relatively uncommon in that it slowly undergoes post-translational deamidation in vivo to form aspartic acid, with the latter residue (β82Asp) comprising ~67–75% in mature mixed blood (Bardakjian et al., 1985; Perutz et al., 1980).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on Hb Providence.

claims.claim: The deamidation reaction of Asn to Asp is dependent on two nearby residues β143His and β83Gly.
claims.source: Additionally, this reaction is dependent on the local protein environment (Robinson, 2002), specifically two nearby residues β143His and β83Gly (Perutz et al., 1980).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on protein deamidation.

claims.claim: The β/δ83Gly residue was replaced by β/δ83Ser on the Steller's sea cow branch, which is expected to slow the rate of deamidation.
claims.source: Importantly, the latter residue was replaced by β/δ83Ser on the Steller's sea cow branch (Figures 1B and 3B), which is expected to slow (but not stop) the rate of deamidation (Robinson, 2002).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through sequence data and supported by citation on deamidation kinetics.

claims.claim: The two Hb Providence isoforms (β82Asn and β82Asp) have similar O2 affinities and functional properties.
claims.source: Regardless, since the two Hb Providence isoforms have similar O2 affinities and functional properties (Bardakjian et al., 1985; Bonaventura et al., 1976; Charache et al., 1977) it is unlikely that the presence of β/δ82Asp in the Steller's sea cow blood would meaningfully alter the results and interpretations presented herein.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on Hb Providence.

claims.claim: Steller's sea cows had a gestational period of approximately 1 year.
claims.source: This value is ~10–50 times the mass of newborn manatees and dugongs (~10–50 kg) (Odell, 2009) and is suggestive of rapid prenatal growth during the ~1 year gestational period indicated by Steller (Steller, 1751).
claims.evidence: This is based on historical account by Steller cited in the text.

claims.claim: Steller's sea cows kept their heads always under water while foraging without regard to life and safety.
claims.source: Although this species was presumably unable to completely submerge (Domning, 2022; Steller, 1751), this conjecture is corroborated by Steller's account that, 'they keep their heads always under water [foraging], without regard to life and safety' (Steller, 1751).
claims.evidence: This is based on historical observations by Steller cited in the text.

claims.claim: Steller observed that Steller's sea cow flesh could be kept in the open air for a very long time without any bad odor, even though full of maggots.
claims.source: A reduced potential for Hb oxidation may also help explain Steller's vexing observation that 'what is remarkable, even in the hottest days it [the flesh] can be kept in the open air for a very long time without any bad odor, even though all full of worms [maggots]' (Steller, 1751).
claims.evidence: This is based on historical observations by Steller cited in the text.

claims.claim: Countercurrent rete supplying the flippers and tail flukes are well developed in manatees and presumably other sirenians.
claims.source: The inferred reduction in insulative blubber thickness of H. gigas during the winter months would likely have compounded the rate of heat loss to sub-zero degree Celsius air and water, though may have been compensated for by arteriovenous anastomoses that regulated blood flow to the skin, and by countercurrent rete supplying the flippers and tail flukes, the latter of which are well developed in manatees and presumably other sirenians (Marshall et al., 2022; Rommel and Caplan, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claims.claim: Steller observed that when Steller's sea cows kept their heads underwater the blood did not flow out from wounds, but when they raised their heads to breathe the blood leaped forth anew.
claims.source: Indeed, Steller inadvertently was the first to (indirectly) describe this phenomenon as he observed his crew hunting the animals with spears and knives, 'the blood from the wounded back spurted up like a fountain. As long as he kept his head underwater the blood did not flow out, but as soon as he raised his head to breathe the blood leaped forth anew' (Steller, 1751).
claims.evidence: This is based on historical observations by Steller cited in the text.

claims.claim: The timing of globin gene expression is determined by its distance from the locus control region.
claims.source: Given that the timing of globin gene expression is determined by its distance from the locus control region (Peterson and Stamatoyannopoulos, 1993), the possible attenuation of HBG expression in sirenians HBG relative to elephants is supported by synteny comparisons of the β-globin gene cluster, as the HBG locus of sirenians is further downstream than the same locus is in the elephant cluster (see Figure 1B of Signore et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous study and comparison with previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: The HBG locus of sirenians is further downstream than the same locus is in the elephant cluster.
claims.source: Given that the timing of globin gene expression is determined by its distance from the locus control region (Peterson and Stamatoyannopoulos, 1993), the possible attenuation of HBG expression in sirenians HBG relative to elephants is supported by synteny comparisons of the β-globin gene cluster, as the HBG locus of sirenians is further downstream than the same locus is in the elephant cluster (see Figure 1B of Signore et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is based on synteny comparisons from previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: Fetal blood cells expressing HbA contain only trace amounts of DPG, conferring fetal blood with an elevated O2 affinity relative to maternal circulation in the vast majority of mammalian species.
claims.source: Presumably, to assist in this process, fetal blood cells expressing HbA contain only trace amounts of DPG hence conferring fetal blood with an elevated O2 affinity relative to that of the maternal circulation (compare the dashed vs. solid red lines in Figure 4A as an example) in the vast majority of mammalian species (Bunn, 1980; Carter, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous reviews and illustrated in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Steller's sea cows represent a rare example in which fetal and maternal blood has the same O2 affinity due to inability to respond to DPG.
claims.source: By contrast, and owing to the inability of Steller's sea cows Hb to respond to DPG in either the fetal or adult circulations, this species would represent a rare example (feloids and eastern moles are others) in which fetal and maternal blood has the same (albeit relatively low) O2 affinity.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing DPG insensitivity.

claims.claim: Placental O2 delivery in Steller's sea cows was defended by the double Bohr effect.
claims.source: However, placental O2 delivery in these species will be defended by the well-known double Bohr effect, whereby CO2 transport from the fetal to maternal circulation increases blood O2 affinity in the former while lowering it in the latter (Carter, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is based on established physiological knowledge cited from literature.

claims.claim: The evolved reduction in blood O2 affinity of Steller's sea cows stipulated that equilibrium between umbilical and uterine blood was reached at a higher PO2.
claims.source: More importantly, the evolved reduction in blood O2 affinity of Steller's sea cows would have stipulated that equilibrium between umbilical and uterine blood was reached at a higher PO2, a condition that is expected to substantially improve O2 delivery to the fetal circulation (Carter, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the functional properties measured and supported by citation.

claims.claim: The lower fetal blood O2 affinity of Steller's sea cows would have augmented O2 delivery to developing tissues.
claims.source: The lower fetal blood O2 affinity (relative to manatees and dugongs) and concomitant higher fetal blood-to-tissue PO2 gradients are further expected to have augmented O2 delivery to the developing tissues of this species.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the functional properties measured experimentally.

claims.claim: Increases in Hb solubility/reduced susceptibility to oxidative damage arising from β/δ82Lys→Asn may have elevated the O2 carrying capacity of fetal blood.
claims.source: As such, these attributes, together with increases in Hb solubility/reduced susceptibility to oxidative damage arising from β/δ82Lys→Asn that conceivably also elevated the O2 carrying capacity of fetal blood, may have been important contributors to the enhanced fetal growth rate of these immense sirenians.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the solubility data and comparison with human Hb Providence.

claims.claim: The increase in thermal inertia and relatively low surface-area-to-volume ratio following birth were presumably central components of Steller's sea cows successful exploitation of harsh sub-Arctic marine environments.
claims.source: The resulting increase in thermal inertia and relatively low surface-area-to-volume ratio following birth, together with an adaptively reduced Hb thermal sensitivity and thick 'bark-like' skin arising from the inactivation of lipoxygenase genes (Le Duc et al., 2022), were presumably central components of Steller's sea cows successful exploitation of the harsh sub-Arctic marine environments of the North Pacific.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combination of physiological and morphological traits discussed.

claims.claim: Steller's sea cow thick 'bark-like' skin arose from the inactivation of lipoxygenase genes.
claims.source: The resulting increase in thermal inertia and relatively low surface-area-to-volume ratio following birth, together with an adaptively reduced Hb thermal sensitivity and thick 'bark-like' skin arising from the inactivation of lipoxygenase genes (Le Duc et al., 2022), were presumably central components of Steller's sea cows successful exploitation of the harsh sub-Arctic marine environments of the North Pacific.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous genetic study.

claims.claim: Steller's sea cow and dugong diverged between the mid-Oligocene and early Miocene (21.2-28.6 million years ago).
claims.source: Divergence dates in millions of years (Mya) are based on and Heritage and Seiffert, 2022.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and supported by citation.

results.result: Steller's sea cow hemoglobin harbors a fixed β/δ82Lys→Asn substitution at an otherwise invariant position among mammalian hemoglobins. This substitution was confirmed in 16 individuals from the last remaining population.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, and C19 are well-supported by sequence data shown in Figure 1B demonstrating fixation across 16 individuals, and by sequence conservation analysis (Figure 3A) showing invariance of β82Lys in other mammals. The data provide strong evidence for this unique substitution.

results.result: Steller's sea cow hemoglobin exhibits reduced temperature sensitivity compared to other sirenians, arising from an inherently low enthalpy of oxygenation (ΔH) of the protein. The β82Asn substitution is a key factor underlying this low thermal sensitivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C6, C31-C33 are supported by experimental measurements of enthalpy values (Figure 2B) showing ΔH' of -18.8 kJ/mol for H. gigas compared to -50.1 to -58.6 kJ/mol for other sirenians. Site-directed mutagenesis experiments (C33) demonstrate that reverting β82Asn→Lys increases ΔH, confirming the role of this substitution.

results.result: The β/δ82Lys→Asn substitution renders Steller's sea cow hemoglobin unresponsive to 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (DPG), representing the first documented example of a DPG-insensitive hemoglobin phenotype among mammals. This arises from deletion of the integral DPG binding site at position 82.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C8, C27, C64-C67 are strongly supported by functional assays showing negligible DPG effect (ΔlogP50=0.02) in wild-type H. gigas Hb (Figure 2C), restoration of DPG sensitivity in the β82Asn→Lys mutant, and structural modeling (Figure 3) showing loss of the key DPG binding residue. The claim of being the first mammalian example is supported by comparison with literature.

results.result: Steller's sea cow evolved a secondarily reduced blood-O2 affinity phenotype, with P50 approximately 2-fold higher than ancestral dugongid and extant sirenians. This reduction predominantly arises from the β/δ82Asn substitution and contrasts with allometric expectations for large mammals.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C23, C24, C28-C30 are supported by O2 equilibrium measurements (Figure 2A) showing P50 of 8.8 mm Hg for H. gigas versus 3.5-5.4 mm Hg for other sirenians under stripped conditions. Site-directed mutagenesis (C24) confirms the β82Asn substitution as the primary cause. The evolutionary interpretation is supported by ancestral reconstruction and comparison with allometric expectations.

results.result: The β/δ82Lys→Asn substitution increases hemoglobin solubility in Steller's sea cow, potentially reducing oxidative damage and increasing protein half-life. This is demonstrated through ammonium sulfate precipitation assays and is consistent with observations in human Hb Providence.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C75-C78 are supported by experimental solubility assays (Figure 2F) showing less precipitation of H. gigas Hb compared to other sirenians and the β82Asn→Lys mutant. The mechanism is supported by citations to studies on human Hb Providence showing reduced oxidative damage at β93Cys and increased protein stability.

results.result: The β82Asn substitution uncouples thermal sensitivity from DPG concentration through genetic assimilation, permanently conferring low ΔH' while eliminating the energetic cost of DPG production.
results.evaluation: Claims C34 and C86 are supported by experimental data showing similar ΔH' values for wild-type and mutant H. gigas Hb in the presence of allosteric effectors despite different intrinsic ΔH values (Figure 2B). This demonstrates that the low thermal sensitivity is maintained without requiring DPG, supporting the genetic assimilation hypothesis.

results.result: Steller's sea cow fetal hemoglobin (HbF) contains rare γ-chain replacements (γ38Thr→Ile and γ101Glu→Asp) that increased O2 affinity relative to dugong HbF. These substitutions alter key structural interfaces and are predicted to affect protein function.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C55-C57, C60-C62 are supported by O2 equilibrium measurements (Figure 4A) showing P50 of 0.56 mm Hg for H. gigas HbF versus 1.2 mm Hg for dugong HbF. Structural modeling (Figure 4B-E) demonstrates the locations and predicted effects of these substitutions on the α1γ2 sliding interface and heme contacts. The functional measurements are consistent with the structural predictions.

results.result: The HBG transcriptional control motif (CACCC) crucial for fetal suppression of HBB is mutated in dugongids, indicating that HbA is likely the primary hemoglobin isoform expressed in both fetal and postnatal circulation. The HBG locus position in sirenians is further downstream than in elephants.
results.evaluation: Claims C58, C59, C96, C97 are supported by sequence analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) showing mutation of the CACCC motif in dugongids but not manatees or elephants. The inference about HbA expression (C59) is logical given the loss of the suppression motif. The synteny comparison (C97) is supported by citation to previous work.

results.result: Despite possessing identical DPG binding site residues as human Hb Providence, H. gigas Hb exhibits a distinctly lower DPG effect, implicating epistatic contributions from other amino acids. The direction and magnitude of the β82Asn substitution's effect is conditional on genetic background.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 are supported by comparison of experimental measurements with literature values for human Hb Providence, showing different functional outcomes despite identical residues at position 82. This demonstrates epistasis and context-dependence of substitution effects, supported by citations to recent research on this phenomenon.

results.result: Extant sirenian hemoglobins (dugong, manatee) exhibit normal allosteric effector sensitivity, with O2 affinity reduced in the presence of Cl− and DPG to levels similar to Asian elephant Hb. The high blood-O2 affinity of these species is not due to decreased allosteric effector sensitivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C27 are supported by experimental measurements showing similar DPG and Cl− effects in dugong, ancestral dugongid, and manatee Hbs compared to Asian elephant (Figure 2C-D). This extends previous studies and clarifies that high blood-O2 affinity in extant sirenians arises from intrinsic properties rather than altered allosteric regulation.

results.result: The reduced blood-O2 affinity in Steller's sea cow would have augmented tissue and fetal O2 delivery. Despite fetal and maternal blood having the same O2 affinity due to DPG insensitivity, placental O2 delivery would be defended by the double Bohr effect, with equilibrium reached at higher PO2.
results.evaluation: Claims C44, C99-C102 are supported by the functional measurements showing reduced O2 affinity and DPG insensitivity. The physiological inferences about O2 delivery are logical extensions of the data and are supported by citations to established physiological principles. The prediction about fetal-maternal gas exchange is consistent with the measured Hb properties.

results.result: Previous phylogenetic analyses failed to detect positive selection or accelerated substitution rates in Steller's sea cow globin genes, despite marked functional changes. This pattern is also observed in woolly mammoths and stem penguins.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36 are supported by citations to previous phylogenetic studies. This represents an important observation about the limitations of selection tests in detecting functionally important changes, though it relies entirely on prior work rather than new analyses.

results.result: Species with suppressed DPG sensitivity have markedly reduced red blood cell DPG concentrations (<0.1-1.0 mM vs. 4-10 mM). Approximately 20% of glucose uptake in human erythrocytes is diverted to DPG synthesis, with each DPG molecule produced at the expense of one ATP molecule.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C74 are supported by citations to previous studies on erythrocyte metabolism and DPG concentrations. The biochemical relationship between DPG and ATP production is well-established. The inference that Steller's sea cow likely had low DPG levels (C74) is logical given the DPG insensitivity.

results.result: The enthalpy of heme oxygenation (ΔHO2) is invariantly exothermic (-59 kJ/mol), creating an inverse relationship between temperature and Hb-O2 affinity. Low ΔH' values are adaptive for cold-tolerant mammals and can arise from either increased heterotropic ligand binding or positive ΔHT→R.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C85 are supported by citations to thermodynamic studies and comparative work on other cold-adapted species (woolly mammoth, deer mouse, cow, shrew, mole). This provides important context for interpreting the Steller's sea cow results and represents established knowledge in the field.

results.result: Extant sirenians do not exhibit elevated body O2 stores common to other marine mammals. Their secondary transition to aquatic life coincided with rapid Hb gene evolution due to gene conversion events, resulting in high blood-O2 affinity that maximizes lung O2 extraction. Limited thermoregulatory capacity confines them to (sub)tropical waters, and they lack non-shivering thermogenesis due to UCP1 pseudogenization.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C15, C17 are supported by citations to previous studies on sirenian physiology, genetics, and distribution. These provide important background context for understanding the unique adaptations of Steller's sea cow, though they represent prior knowledge rather than new findings.

results.result: Historical accounts and anatomical studies document Steller's sea cow morphology and behavior, including thick bark-like hide, fingerless forelimbs, toothless jaws with keratinized pads, proportionally larger gut, immense size (up to 11,000 kg), large calves (~544 kg), and short submergence times (4-5 min). These features are consistent with high energetic requirements and cold adaptation.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C48, C91-C95 are supported by citations to historical accounts (primarily Steller, 1751) and anatomical studies. While these are not new findings, they provide essential context for interpreting the hemoglobin adaptations. The inferences about energetic requirements (C42) are logical given the anatomical observations.

results.result: Mammalian embryonic development involves temporal switching of hemoglobin isoforms with successively lower O2 affinities to facilitate maternal-fetal O2 transfer. In most mammals except bovids and simian primates, embryonic Hb expression is limited to the embryonic stage. Fetal blood cells expressing HbA contain trace DPG, conferring elevated O2 affinity relative to maternal circulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C54, C98 are supported by citations to previous studies on mammalian development and hemoglobin switching. These represent established knowledge that provides context for interpreting the sirenian prenatal hemoglobin results, though they are not new findings from this study.

results.result: Human Hb Providence (β82Lys→Asn) exhibits decreased inherent O2 affinity and reduced allosteric effector sensitivity. The β82Asn residue undergoes slow post-translational deamidation to Asp (~67-75% in mature blood), dependent on nearby β143His and β83Gly. In Steller's sea cow, β83Ser replacement is expected to slow deamidation, though the two isoforms have similar functional properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C20, C87-C90 are supported by citations to studies on human Hb Providence. The inference about slower deamidation in H. gigas (C89) is supported by sequence data (Figures 1B, 3B) and citation on deamidation kinetics. The conclusion that deamidation would not meaningfully alter results (C90) is reasonable given literature on Hb Providence.

results.result: The mRNA capping site of H. gigas HbF exhibits an A→G transversion mutation that has been shown to lower transcript levels of human HBB by twofold.
results.evaluation: Claim C63 is supported by sequence analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) showing the mutation and citation to a human study demonstrating the functional effect. However, the actual effect on H. gigas HbF expression is unknown, limiting the interpretation of this finding.

results.result: Humans carrying β82 substitutions exhibit mild polycythemia. Elevated blood O2 carrying capacity is typical of most mammalian divers but is not observed in extant sirenians.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81 are supported by citations to clinical and physiological studies. These provide context for interpreting the potential effects of increased Hb solubility in Steller's sea cow, though they represent prior knowledge rather than new findings.

results.result: Increases in Hb solubility and reduced oxidative damage from β/δ82Lys→Asn may have elevated fetal blood O2 carrying capacity and contributed to enhanced fetal growth rates. Combined with increased thermal inertia, low surface-area-to-volume ratio, reduced Hb thermal sensitivity, and thick skin from lipoxygenase gene inactivation, these adaptations enabled successful exploitation of sub-Arctic environments.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C105 involve speculative inferences about fetal growth and cold adaptation. While C103 is explicitly marked as speculative ('conceivably', 'may have been'), and C104-C105 use cautious language ('presumably'), the connections between Hb properties and fetal growth rates lack direct experimental support. The thick skin mechanism (C105) is supported by citation, but the overall synthesis remains inferential.

results.result: Steller's sea cow (Hydrodamalis gigas) was a whale-sized marine mammal that became extinct in 1768. They persisted in the North Pacific from the Miocene (5-8 million years ago) until extinction. Steller's sea cow and dugong diverged between the mid-Oligocene and early Miocene (21.2-28.6 million years ago).
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C16, C106 are supported by historical records and citations to fossil evidence and phylogenetic studies. These provide essential background information about the species, though they represent established knowledge rather than new findings.

results.result: Steller's sea cow Hb accumulated 11 amino acid replacements since its divergence from the dugong.
results.evaluation: Claim C18 is supported by sequence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citation to previous work. This provides important context for understanding which substitutions are responsible for functional changes.
